name: Economics
title: Economist
blurb: Strategy consultants and markets-systems people are expected to read GDP prints, BoJ decisions and yen moves fluently, and this gives Arin that language.

chapters.title: Supply, demand and elasticity
chapters.read: An introductory microeconomics textbook's chapters on supply and demand, equilibrium, price controls and price elasticity (including the midpoint method and the link between elasticity and total revenue).
chapters.produce: Pick three products you buy in Kofu (e.g. rice, train tickets, coffee) and write a one-page note on each: what shifts its demand and supply, and whether its demand is likely elastic or inelastic and why.

quiz.q: Rice is a normal good. Household incomes in Japan rise. What happens in the rice market, all else equal?
opts: The demand curve shifts to the right
The demand curve shifts to the left
There is a movement down along the demand curve
The supply curve shifts to the right
quiz.ex: Income changes shift the whole demand curve; for a normal good, higher income means more demanded at every price.

quiz.q: The price of a bento rises from ¥200 to ¥220 and quantity demanded falls from 1,000 to 850 a day. Using percentage changes from the starting values, what is the price elasticity of demand (absolute value)?
Demand is Qd = 100 − 2P and supply is Qs = 20 + 2P. What is the equilibrium price P?
Demand for a product is price-inelastic (|elasticity| < 1). If the seller raises the price, total revenue will…
opts: Fall
Rise
Stay exactly the same
Become zero because demand collapses
quiz.ex: With inelastic demand, quantity falls proportionally less than price rises, so P × Q goes up.

quiz.q: The government sets a legal maximum rent below the market equilibrium rent. What is the most likely result?
opts: A surplus of rental flats
No effect, because ceilings below equilibrium are non-binding
A shortage of rental flats
A rightward shift of the supply curve
quiz.ex: A binding price ceiling raises quantity demanded and lowers quantity supplied, creating a shortage.

quiz.q: Using the midpoint (arc) method: price rises from ¥100 to ¥120 and quantity demanded falls from 500 to 400. What is the absolute price elasticity of demand? (2 decimal places)

chapters.title: Market structures
chapters.read: A microeconomics textbook's chapters on costs, perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly, focusing on the MR = MC rule, entry/exit and market-concentration measures such as HHI.
chapters.produce: Write a 1-page 'industry structure' slide for a Japanese industry you can observe (convenience stores, mobile carriers or ramen shops): number of players, product differentiation, barriers to entry, and which model fits best.

quiz.q: Which rule does a profit-maximising firm follow when choosing output, in every market structure?
opts: Produce where total revenue is highest
Produce where price equals average cost
Produce where average cost is lowest
Produce where marginal revenue equals marginal cost
quiz.ex: Profit rises as long as an extra unit adds more revenue than cost, so it peaks where MR = MC.

quiz.q: In long-run equilibrium under perfect competition, a typical firm earns…
opts: Zero economic profit
Large economic profits protected by barriers to entry
Negative economic profit permanently
Monopoly profits from product differentiation
quiz.ex: Free entry and exit push price to minimum average cost, so economic profit is driven to zero.

quiz.q: Which feature best defines an oligopoly?
opts: Many small firms selling identical products
A few large firms whose decisions depend on each other's
One seller with no close substitutes
Many firms each selling a slightly different product with free entry
quiz.ex: Oligopoly means few sellers and strategic interdependence (e.g. Japan's mobile carriers).

quiz.q: A street with dozens of ramen shops, each with its own style of soup, and easy entry for new shops is best described as…
opts: Perfect competition
Monopoly
Monopolistic competition
Oligopoly
quiz.ex: Many sellers + differentiated products + free entry is the textbook definition of monopolistic competition.

quiz.q: A firm in a perfectly competitive market sells 1,000 units at the market price of ¥300. Its average total cost at that output is ¥250. What is its economic profit?
An industry has four firms with market shares of 40%, 30%, 20% and 10%. What is its Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI), using shares in percent?

chapters.title: GDP and the national accounts
chapters.read: A macroeconomics textbook's chapters on measuring GDP (expenditure, income and value-added approaches), nominal vs real GDP, the GDP deflator and GNI; then skim the structure of a Cabinet Office quarterly GDP release (速報) to see the components in practice.
chapters.produce: Build a small spreadsheet that takes C, I, G, X and M plus a deflator and outputs nominal GDP, real GDP and the growth rate, then write three sentences interpreting a made-up quarter.

quiz.q: An economy has (in trillion ¥): consumption 300, investment 100, government purchases 120, exports 80, imports 60. What is GDP?
Nominal GDP is ¥550 trillion and the GDP deflator is 110 (base year = 100). What is real GDP?
quiz.ex: Real GDP = nominal ÷ (deflator/100) = 550 ÷ 1.10 = 500.

quiz.q: Real GDP rises from ¥500 trillion to ¥515 trillion over a year. What is the real growth rate?
Which of these is NOT counted in GDP?
opts: A new machine bought by a factory
Cars made in Japan and sold abroad
Government spending on a new bridge
A government pension payment to a retiree
quiz.ex: Pensions are transfer payments: they redistribute income but pay for no new output, so they are excluded.

quiz.q: How does gross national income (GNI) differ from GDP?
opts: GNI adds net primary income (e.g. wages, interest, dividends) received from abroad
GNI subtracts depreciation from GDP
GNI subtracts taxes from GDP
GNI adds imports to GDP
quiz.ex: GDP measures production inside the country; GNI measures income of residents, so it adds net income flows from abroad.

quiz.q: A farmer sells wheat to a miller for ¥100, the miller sells flour to a baker for ¥250, and the baker sells bread to consumers for ¥600. How much does this chain add to GDP?
quiz.ex: Only final goods count (or sum value added: 100 + 150 + 350 = 600).

chapters.title: Money, central banks and the BoJ's tools
chapters.read: A macroeconomics textbook's chapters on money, banking and monetary policy (money creation, the policy rate, open market operations), then the Bank of Japan's own explainer pages on its policy tools as concepts: policy-rate setting, quantitative easing, negative interest rates and yield curve control.
chapters.produce: Write a one-page explainer, as if for a client, of how a central-bank bond purchase flows through bank reserves, short- and long-term interest rates, and the yen; include a simple diagram.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the standard functions of money?
opts: Medium of exchange
Guaranteeing a positive real return
Unit of account
Store of value
quiz.ex: Money's three textbook functions are medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value; it guarantees no real return (inflation can erode it).

quiz.q: In the simple money-multiplier model, banks keep 10% of deposits as reserves and lend the rest; all loans are redeposited. A new deposit of ¥1,000,000 arrives. What is the maximum total deposits it can support?
When a central bank buys government bonds from banks in an open market operation, it typically…
opts: Decreases bank reserves and raises interest rates
Has no effect on reserves, only on the exchange rate
Increases bank reserves and puts downward pressure on interest rates
Raises the reserve requirement automatically
quiz.ex: Paying for the bonds credits banks' reserve accounts, adding liquidity and pushing rates down.

quiz.q: As a concept, 'yield curve control' means the central bank…
opts: Only sets the overnight interest rate and lets all other yields float
Fixes the exchange rate against the US dollar
Sets the interest rates banks charge on mortgages by law
Targets a longer-term government bond yield and stands ready to buy bonds to hold it near the target
quiz.ex: YCC extends control from the short end to a longer maturity by committing to buy (or sell) bonds around a yield target.

quiz.q: Under a negative policy interest rate, as a concept…
opts: Banks are charged for holding certain reserves at the central bank
Households are legally required to pay interest on all deposits
The central bank pays banks extra interest on all reserves
Government bonds can no longer be traded
quiz.ex: A negative rate on (some tier of) reserves penalises idle balances, aiming to push banks to lend or invest.

quiz.q: A zero-coupon bond pays ¥1,000 in one year and costs ¥980 today. What is its one-year yield? (2 decimal places)
quiz.ex: 1,000/980 − 1 = 0.020408 ≈ 2.04%. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

chapters.title: Inflation, unemployment and exchange rates
chapters.read: A macroeconomics textbook's chapters on price indices (CPI), real vs nominal interest rates (Fisher equation), labour-market statistics and the Phillips curve, plus an open-economy chapter on exchange rates and purchasing power parity.
chapters.produce: Make a two-column table, 'weak yen' vs 'strong yen', listing effects on exporters, importers, tourists, households and the CPI, and write one paragraph on who in Kofu wins or loses.

quiz.q: The CPI rises from 105.0 to 108.15 in a year. What is the inflation rate?
A country has 66.0 million employed, 1.8 million unemployed and 40 million adults not in the labour force. What is the unemployment rate? (2 decimal places)
quiz.ex: Unemployed ÷ labour force = 1.8/(66.0 + 1.8) = 1.8/67.8 ≈ 2.65%. People outside the labour force are excluded.

quiz.q: A deposit pays a nominal interest rate of 0.5% while inflation is 2.5%. Using the approximate Fisher relation, what is the real interest rate?
quiz.ex: Real ≈ nominal − inflation = 0.5 − 2.5 = −2%.

quiz.q: The exchange rate moves from ¥150 per US dollar to ¥130 per US dollar. The yen has…
opts: Depreciated
Appreciated
Been devalued
Stayed unchanged in value
quiz.ex: Fewer yen are needed to buy one dollar, so each yen is worth more: the yen has appreciated.

quiz.q: All else equal, a weaker yen tends to…
opts: Make imports cheaper in yen
Lower the yen price of imported oil
Make Japanese exports cheaper abroad and imports more expensive in yen
Make foreign holidays cheaper for Japanese tourists
quiz.ex: Depreciation lowers the foreign-currency price of Japanese goods and raises the yen cost of foreign goods.

quiz.q: The short-run Phillips curve describes…
opts: A positive relationship between GDP and imports
The link between money supply and exchange rates
A positive relationship between inflation and unemployment in every period
An inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment
quiz.ex: In the short run, lower unemployment tends to come with higher inflation, and vice versa.

chapters.title: Trade and Japan's economy
chapters.read: A textbook chapter on comparative advantage, tariffs and trade policy, then an overview of Japan's economic structure from a government white paper or an international organisation's country survey: demographics, energy dependence, manufacturing and the long period of low inflation.
chapters.produce: Write a 2-page 'Japan macro primer' a new consultant could read in 10 minutes: five structural facts, why each matters for clients, and one chart you draw yourself from published data.

quiz.q: In Japan, one worker can make either 4 robots or 8 tonnes of rice per month. What is the opportunity cost of one robot, in tonnes of rice?
quiz.ex: Giving up 8 tonnes for 4 robots means 8/4 = 2 tonnes of rice per robot.

quiz.q: A country has a comparative advantage in a good when it…
opts: Can produce it at a lower opportunity cost than its trading partner
Can produce more of it per worker than any other country
Exports more of it than any other country
Has a government subsidy for it
quiz.ex: Comparative advantage is about lower opportunity cost, not absolute productivity (that is absolute advantage).

quiz.q: Which best describes Japan's long-run demographic trend since around the late 2000s?
opts: The population is growing quickly through high birth rates
The total population is shrinking and ageing
The population is stable with a young median age
The working-age share is rising fast
quiz.ex: Low fertility and long life expectancy mean Japan's population has been falling and ageing for over a decade.

quiz.q: Which structural fact about Japan's economy is most relevant to why a weak yen raises household energy bills?
opts: Japan is a major net exporter of crude oil
Japan generates nearly all its energy from domestic coal mines
Japan imports most of its energy (oil, LNG, coal)
Japan prices all its energy imports in yen
quiz.ex: With few domestic energy resources, Japan buys fuel abroad, largely priced in dollars, so a weaker yen raises yen costs.

quiz.q: A country imposes a tariff on imported beef. Compared with free trade, which outcome is expected?
opts: Domestic beef prices fall and consumers gain
Imports rise because foreign beef becomes more attractive
There is no change in domestic prices
Domestic beef prices rise, helping domestic producers but hurting consumers
quiz.ex: The tariff raises the domestic price; producers and the government gain, consumers lose more, leaving a deadweight loss.

quiz.q: A country imports 2,000 units of a good at a world price of ¥500 each and imposes a 20% ad valorem tariff. Assuming imports stay at 2,000 units, how much tariff revenue is collected?

boss.q: The price elasticity of demand for train passes is −0.4. If the price rises by 10%, by approximately what percentage does quantity demanded fall?
An economy has C = 320, I = 110, G = 130, X = 100 and M = 120 (trillion ¥), and the GDP deflator is 108. What is real GDP?
Compared with a perfectly competitive industry facing the same costs, a monopoly typically…
opts: Produces less, charges a higher price and creates a deadweight loss
Produces more and charges a lower price
Produces the same quantity but at a higher price, with no efficiency loss
Earns zero economic profit in the long run because of free entry
boss.ex: A monopolist sets MR = MC where MR < P, restricting output below the efficient level.

boss.q: All else equal, if the Bank of Japan raises its policy rate while the US Federal Reserve leaves its rate unchanged, the yen would be expected to…
opts: Depreciate against the dollar
Appreciate against the dollar
Remain fixed because Japan pegs the yen
Move only if Japan's trade balance changes first
boss.ex: A narrower rate gap makes yen assets relatively more attractive, raising demand for yen.

boss.q: Nominal GDP grows 4% in a year and the GDP deflator rises 1.5%. Using the simple approximation, what is real GDP growth?
boss.ex: Real growth ≈ nominal growth − deflator inflation = 4 − 1.5 = 2.5% (exactly 1.04/1.015 − 1 ≈ 2.46%).

boss.q: A sudden jump in oil prices raises costs across the economy. Which combination is most likely in the short run?
opts: Lower inflation and lower unemployment
Higher output and falling prices
Higher inflation together with lower output and higher unemployment
No change in inflation but higher output
boss.ex: A negative supply shock shifts aggregate supply left, producing stagflation.

boss.q: The price of coffee rises 10% and the quantity of tea demanded rises 5%. What is the cross-price elasticity of demand for tea with respect to coffee's price?
boss.ex: 5%/10% = +0.5. The positive sign means tea and coffee are substitutes.

boss.q: Which of these is a stock rather than a flow?
opts: The government budget deficit for the year
GDP
Annual household consumption
Government debt outstanding
boss.ex: Debt is measured at a point in time (a stock); deficits, GDP and consumption are measured per period (flows).

boss.q: A burger costs ¥480 in Japan and $6.00 in the US. What exchange rate (¥ per $) would make the burger cost the same in both places (the PPP rate)?
Why do central banks generally regard persistent deflation as harmful?
opts: Falling prices raise the real burden of debt and can lead people to delay spending
Deflation always raises real wages so firms hire more
Deflation makes nominal interest rates negative automatically
Deflation reduces the real value of savings
boss.ex: Debts are fixed in nominal terms, so falling prices make them heavier, and expected price falls encourage postponed purchases.
